title: Reinforced Concrete Column, Beam and Slab Defects Homeowners Should Know
desc: Common defects in building reinforced concrete columns, beams and slabs in houses: formwork, reinforcement, cover, joints, early stripping, and how to check.
summary: A roundup of common defects in building the reinforced concrete frame of a house and a list of what homeowners should check before concrete is poured.
body: p

The reinforced concrete frame (columns, beams, slabs) is the “skeleton” of the house. Most cracking, sagging and leaking in private homes comes from construction errors rather than design. Homeowners do not need to be engineers, but knowing the common defects helps them supervise better.
h2
1. Formwork and shoring defects
ul
Formwork that is not tight and has gaps lets cement paste leak out, leaving honeycombed concrete with exposed reinforcement.
Formwork that is not straight or the right size makes columns lean and beams misaligned.
Weak shoring set on soft ground leads to slabs sagging as soon as concrete is poured.
Removing formwork and props too early, before the concrete has reached enough strength – a common cause of sagging and slab cracks.
h2
2. Reinforcement defects
ul
Wrong quantity, diameter or spacing of bars compared with the drawings.
Bars spliced in the wrong place, lap lengths insufficient under the design, or many splices concentrated in the same cross-section.
Bars trampled flat or displaced by foot traffic and the concrete pour, especially the top load-bearing bars at beam supports and in slabs.
Missing spacers, leaving bars against the formwork with insufficient concrete cover, so they rust easily and the concrete spalls later.
Dirty bars, stained with oil, mud or heavy rust, reducing bond.
h2
3. Defects in pouring and curing concrete
ul
Adding water on one's own to make the concrete “easier to pour”, which reduces strength.
Poor or excessive vibration causing honeycombing and segregation.
Stopping the pour midway (construction joint) at a position not permitted by the engineer.
Not wetting and covering the concrete after pouring, especially in hot sun, causing surface cracks.
h2
4. What should the homeowner check before concrete is poured?
ol
Compare the quantity and size of bars with the drawings; take photos of each location for the record.
Check the spacers and the gap between bars and formwork.
Check that formwork is tight and firm; shoring is adequate and set on firm ground.
Electrical conduits and water pipes in the slab are laid correctly, with no load-bearing bars cut.
There is a plan for a continuous pour: enough people, enough materials, and weather contingency.
p

Under Clauses 3 and 4, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP, the owner of a detached house organizes construction and construction supervision and is responsible for safety; supervision covers the quality of materials and components before they are used in construction, the scaffolding system, temporary support structures and safety measures. The acceptance result for each work item should be recorded in minutes, including the name of the work, the time, the participants and a conclusion of accepted or not (Clause 4, Article 22). See also Is hiring construction supervision mandatory when building a house?.
h2
5. What to do when a defect is found?
ul
Before pouring: require the contractor to fix it immediately and re-accept before pouring.
After pouring: do not chip or break it out yourself; invite a structural engineer to inspect, assess and propose a remedy.
Keep photos, logs and minutes as a basis for responsibility and warranty.
p
